summary:
Madhya Pradesh has no state-specific transgender statute and no documented state-level enforcement series of its own, so a visitor to the state is assessed against India's national framework, which applies uniformly across the country.

That framework changed on 25 March 2026, when India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill, approved by both houses and awaiting presidential assent at the time of sourcing. Passage coincided with protests in Mumbai.

The amendment removes the self-identification right affirmed by the Supreme Court in 2014 and limits legal recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme.

Recognition and surgery are tied to documentation. The amended 2019 law makes certification by a medical board and a district authority mandatory before gender-affirming surgery, replacing self-declaration.

The amendment also creates offences for coercing or alluring a person into being transgender, punishable by up to life imprisonment.

The baseline for entry and stay remains mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, which the Supreme Court has held covers gender identity; the Allahabad High Court extended that in 2021 to bar employment discrimination on sexual orientation grounds. There is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had protected trans persons from sexual violence, and trans people fear a rise in assaults because the new code omits them.

Identity documents and checkpoints are a live source of friction. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person who had been asked to take a medical exam by passport authorities. In November 2024 an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, was stopped at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 by Central Industrial Security Force personnel despite presenting her PAN card. In Kolkata a transwoman alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her at the station under the pretext of checking her gender, and transgender persons arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam have recounted degrading treatment in custody.
tangentialFactors:
The March 2026 passage drew street protest in Mumbai, and the People's Union for Civil Liberties warns that the new offences echo colonial-era criminalisation of transgender people. The government presents the amendment as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking; critics say it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

Assessments of police conduct diverge. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic, while victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police.

Protection machinery exists but sits largely outside Madhya Pradesh. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. Bans from that judgment and from the National Medical Commission in 2022 coexist with clandestine networks still operating.

Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha run transgender welfare boards coordinating housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions, and several states provide targeted welfare, housing and healthcare benefits for hijras. Madhya Pradesh is not among the states named in the sources as running such a board.
localsOnly:
Residents of Madhya Pradesh obtain legal recognition through the medical-board and district-authority certification route introduced by the 2026 amendment, rather than by self-declaration.

Nationally, the Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community, including residents of Madhya Pradesh.

In August 2024 the Ministry of Finance clarified that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries.

The new offences for coercing or alluring a person into being transgender, carrying up to life imprisonment, apply within the state under the amended 2019 law.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill received presidential assent after passage on 25 March 2026 is unresolved; the sources record it as awaiting assent.

No Madhya Pradesh welfare board, state housing or pension scheme for transgender residents, or state-level enforcement record appears in the sources. The state's own facilities and care access are not sourced.

No police-conduct assessment specific to Madhya Pradesh appears in the sources; the foreign-government assessment and the victim interviews cover other states.

The Madras High Court order of April 2019 banning sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants binds Tamil Nadu only. No equivalent order for Madhya Pradesh is sourced, and the documented history of infanticide and parental preference for assigning intersex infants male is a national rather than a state-specific finding.
